The DPA fined a telecommunications company €200,000 for issuing a duplicate e-SIM card to an unauthorised person without a valid legal basis.

The Italian DPA inspected Menarini Silicon Biosystems, which was training an AI tool (CellFind) to classify multiple myeloma tumour cells using pseudonymised patient data collected via a Bulgarian processor and data received from a US group company. It found breaches of transparency and the duty to give complete information, storage limitation and accountability, including the lack of a proper assessment of the re-identification risk. It declared the processing unlawful and fined the company EUR 21,000. It ordered the company to state the necessary retention period, submit an amended privacy notice and report how it will publicise the notice. The decision is also published on the Garante's website.
The DPA ordered the provider of DeepSeek AI to appoint a representative in the EU, according to Article 27 GDPR.
The DPA reprimanded a local authority over a data breach. The authority accidentally disclosed a large set of personal data in response to a FOI request.

The DPA held that a customer using the free version of a screen capture software abused his right to access by requesting a copy of his personal data including existing screenshots which are only available to download in the paid version of the software.
A building association was fined €1,000 for posting the minutes of their general assembly containing a list of debtors in the building lobby, in violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.

Romania's data protection authority investigated Maravet S.R.L. after it notified a personal data breach: a former employee copied personal data from the company's database without authorisation and posted it on the website of his new employer. The data of a significant number of people was exposed, including ID numbers, employee records and photos. The authority found the controller had not ensured that persons acting under its authority process data only on its instructions and had not implemented adequate technical and organisational security measures. It fined the controller RON 24,885.50 (about EUR 5,000), which has been paid.

The DPA fined a national credit bureau €200,000 for unlawfully including information regarding a data subject’s unpaid debt in their credit information system and not adequately responding to the data subject’s erasure requests.

ANSPDCP completed an investigation in April 2025 into an accounting and audit consulting company after it notified a personal data breach. Unauthorised persons had illegally accessed personal data of the employees of the company's clients. The authority found that the controller had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures, contrary to Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It imposed a fine of 24,887 lei (about EUR 5,000) and a corrective measure under Article 58(2)(d) to periodically check compliance with data protection procedures and to train staff. The controller has paid the fine.

The CNIL inspected Solocal Marketing Services, a direct-marketing subsidiary of the Solocal group, in October 2022. The company ran email and SMS prospecting campaigns for clients and passed prospect data to clients for postal and telephone marketing, all from a database of about 75 million entries covering some 35 million people. The restricted committee found breaches of Article L. 34-5 of the postal and electronic communications code (consent for electronic prospecting) and of Article 7 GDPR (proof of consent). It also noted a lack of legal basis under Article 6 for part of the data transmitted, but fined only for L. 34-5 CPCE and Article 7. It imposed a fine of EUR 900,000, an injunction to stop electronic prospecting without valid consent with a EUR 10,000 daily penalty after nine months, and publication of the decision, with the company no longer named after two years.

CALOGA, a data broker and e-mail prospecting company holding four prospect databases of over 2.8 million people, was inspected by the CNIL in May 2022. The restricted committee found breaches of Articles 5(1)(e) and 6 GDPR and of Article L. 34-5 of the postal and electronic communications code, because prospecting and transfers of data to partners took place without valid consent or a valid legal basis. The alleged breach of Article 32 (security) was not upheld. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 80,000, taking account of the company's cessation of activity and financial situation, and ordered publication, with the company no longer identifiable after two years.
The DPA clarified that direct marketing and political advertising are distinct and incompatible purposes for processing personal data, and warned a politician over unlawful political advertising.

A job candidate complained that a logistics company required a criminal record certificate for a job interview and handed out a form asking for marital status and number of children. The company argued that air-security rules required the certificate and that the form data was needed for tax withholding (Modelo 145). The AEPD found that both requests were excessive for candidates with no employment relationship and breached the data minimisation principle. It imposed two fines under Article 5(1)(c) GDPR, EUR 75,000 and EUR 25,000, and rejected the request for a mere reprimand.

A person who had been listed in the ASNEF credit information file as guarantor of a mortgage loan complained to the AEPD after a court ruling showed the debt was not owed. The AEPD found the controller, CREDIFIMO, had no legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR for keeping and reporting the data, and proposed a fine of EUR 200,000 and an order to delete the data from ASNEF. CREDIFIMO admitted liability and paid voluntarily, taking two cumulative 20% reductions, so the fine became EUR 120,000 and the procedure was closed.

ANSPDCP concluded an investigation of ROUMASPORT SRL in April 2025, started after complaints. The company accessed the video surveillance system at one of its work points and unlawfully processed images of its employees, including for disciplinary investigations. It was found to have breached Articles 5(1)(a) and (b) and 6(1) GDPR and was fined 24,887 lei (about EUR 5,000). It was also ordered to bring video monitoring into compliance, especially for disciplinary investigations.

The DPA audited the Consulate General of Sweden in Istanbul and ordered it to address security issues related to the processing of physical documents and the verification of the identify of authorized personnel.

The Irish DPC announced its final decision following an inquiry into TikTok's transfers of EEA users' personal data to China, including remote access by staff there, and the transparency of its privacy policy about those transfers. It found that TikTok infringed Article 46(1) GDPR because it did not verify, guarantee and demonstrate essentially equivalent protection, and Article 13(1)(f) GDPR because its 2021 privacy policy did not name the third countries or explain the processing. It imposed fines totalling €530 million (€485 million and €45 million) and ordered TikTok to bring its processing into compliance within 6 months, failing which transfers to China are to be suspended. The DPC also noted that TikTok later reported that some EEA data had in fact been stored on servers in China, contrary to its evidence, and is considering further action.

The CNPD opened an investigation into a Luxembourg engineering company to check compliance with Article 30 GDPR on the record of processing activities. It found that the record was incomplete (missing controller/DPO details, descriptions of data categories and erasure time limits), a breach of Article 30(1)(a), (c) and (f). Treating it as a single, low-gravity infringement under Article 83(4), the restricted panel imposed an administrative fine of EUR 7,000. It declined to order corrective measures because the company had fixed its record after the statement of objections.

The Order of Psychologists of Lombardy notified a ransomware attack in October 2023 by the NoEscape group, in which data were encrypted, exfiltrated and published on the dark web. About 3,000 people and about 15,000 records were affected, including special-category data, criminal-offence data and data covered by professional secrecy. The Garante found that the Order had not put in place adequate measures to detect breaches promptly and to secure the data, in breach of Articles 5(1)(f) and 32(1). It fined the Order EUR 30,000 as a single fine for the combined infringement, and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were imposed because the conduct had ceased and new measures had been adopted.

The Italian DPA inspected the Lombardy Region on its own initiative regarding processing of employee data at work, including remote work. It found unlawful processing of email metadata, internet browsing logs and data in the old OTRS ticketing system, involving breaches of lawfulness, minimisation, storage limitation, data protection by design, DPIA, processor contract and employment-specific rules. It ordered corrective measures on browsing logs within 90 days and imposed separate fines of EUR 20,000, 25,000 and 5,000, totalling EUR 50,000, with publication.
The DPA fined a real estate agency €40,000 for unlawfully processing personal data for direct marketing and for failing to adequately respond to an access request.

The Garante investigated an energy supplier after numerous complaints about unsolicited telemarketing calls, including to numbers on the public opposition register, and about missing replies to data subject rights requests. It found that the company answered the Authority's information requests inadequately and late, failed to identify roles in its sales network (controller/processor), had no valid legal basis or consent for the calls, and mishandled rights requests. It fined the company EUR 100,000, imposed corrective orders including a ban on further processing of the complainants' data, and ordered publication of the decision.

A complaint alleged that a social cooperative, which runs school services for the Municipality of Bologna, emailed the municipality an Excel file with sheets listing children with disabilities and special needs, including their conditions, after an employee's mistake in a strike notice. The Garante found that the cooperative, acting as processor, breached Articles 28(3) and 32(1) GDPR by sending special-category data of vulnerable minors without adequate technical and organisational measures and contrary to the controller's instructions. It fined the cooperative EUR 20,000 and ordered publication of the decision. No further corrective measures were needed because the conduct had ceased to have effect.
The Italian DPA fined a municipality €1,200 for unlawfully publishing the names, birthdates, addresses and social security codes of ten data subjects on its website.

A cooperative working for the Municipality of Bologna sent an email about a strike with an Excel file that accidentally still contained health and disability data of about 60 children in municipal nursery schools. The municipal office forwarded it to all the schools, coordinators and territorial managers, and one school sent it on to 53 parent email addresses. The Garante found that the Municipality processed special-category data without a lawful basis, in breach of Articles 5, 6 and 9 GDPR and the Italian Code. It fined the Municipality EUR 40,000 and ordered publication of the decision, with no further corrective measures because the conduct had ended.
Following an ex officio investigation, the DPA warned a business for failing to provide sufficient information about the cookies on its website.
A data subject’s complaint against Google invoking right to be forgotten under Article 17, was partly upheld by the Italian Data Protection Authority.

The DPA rejected a public officer’s complaint after a news outlet refused to de-index an article about an ongoing criminal investigation against them since the criminal investigation was still ongoing.
The DPA fined a debt collection agency CHF 3,200 (€3,422) for unlawfully publishing information about debtors on its website.

The DPA reprimanded a news outlet for unlawfully processing the data of its website’s visitors after collecting them through cookies. The DPA also clarified that the Post and Telecom authority is the competent enforcer of the e-Privacy Directive's national implementation.

Following complaints, the Romanian DPA investigated a travel company that published on its Facebook page a table of tourists' personal data (names, booking numbers, hotel/location, stay dates) for a prize draw. It found inadequate security measures, failure to notify the personal data breach, and no proof of a full reply to access requests. It fined the company EUR 5,000 for Art. 32 and EUR 1,000 for Art. 33, issued a warning for Art. 15 with Art. 12(3)-(4), and ordered corrective measures on security, breach handling and answering the access request.

The DPA reprimanded a retail company, as well as its data supplier, for unlawfully processing the potential customers’ personal data for direct marketing purposes without having verified the lawfulness of the initial collection. The controller was therefore unable to demonstrate an overriding legitimate interest.

The DPA assessed the FATCA agreement and held that it is not compatible with the GDPR. It reprimanded the Public Federal Service of Finances over several GDPR violations and ordered it to bring its disclosures under FATCA into compliance.

In decision 172/2022 the Belgian Litigation Chamber had ordered a real estate agency to remedy several GDPR infringements and warned it about publishing location data of sold properties. The agency did not appeal or request a hearing on the merits but only partly complied, deliberately keeping some elements online for over two years. The Chamber found non-compliance with the order, punishable under Article 83(6) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 6,000, calculated from a starting point of EUR 5,000 for a one-person company and raised by 20% because the agency persistently refused to give its current turnover.

The Romanian authority finished an investigation in April 2025 into Dante International SA after a customer complained about the processing of email addresses linked to their account on the company's online platform. Although the company confirmed the addresses had been deleted, the complainant still received a feedback message at them, and some of the company's collaborators could view or use the address. The company did not handle the repeated erasure requests properly and gave no clear, transparent information. It was fined 49,770 lei (about EUR 10,000) and ordered to answer the complainant and put technical and organisational measures in place.
The DPA reprimanded a health care provider for sending sensitive data via unencrypted emails, in violation of Article 32(1) GDPR.

The DPA warned the Belgian Post Group for violating the principle of data minimisation. The DPA clarified that the principle applies even when the means of the data processing are explicitly provided for by national law.

The Equality Ombudsman (DO) ran a web form for tips and complaints about discrimination. An analytics tool from a processor was meant to mask free-text entries, but the masking did not work on the form's summary page. Personal data, some of it sensitive or covered by secrecy, was therefore transferred to and stored with the processor for about a year (1 Sept 2020 to 17 Sept 2021). IMY found that DO had not taken appropriate technical and organisational measures under Article 32(1). It rejected a reprimand as too lenient, rated the infringement as low severity, found no aggravating or mitigating factors, and imposed an administrative fine of SEK 100,000.

In a prima facie decision, the DPA warned a company that required consumers to create an account prior to lodging a complaint on its website. The practice does not comply with the principles of minimization and data protection by design and by default

A business manager received direct marketing from a company that had obtained his data from a data broker. He then sent the broker an access request and objected to the processing. The Litigation Chamber found that the broker had no demonstrated legal basis for the processing, did not proactively inform the data subjects, and handled the access request incompletely. It ordered compliance with the access request, erasure of data without a lawful basis, notification of recipients and proactive information. It imposed three fines of EUR 8,000, 6,000 and 6,000 (total EUR 20,000). The Market Court later partly annulled the decision and reduced the fines.
A store was fined €12,000 for failing to implement appropriate access restrictions regarding CCTV footage, in violation of Article 32 GDPR.
The Belgian DPA reprimanded a school for infractions on Article 5.1(a), Article 6.1(e), Article 9.2(a) and clarified the interpretation of Article 8.

In November 2022 police found ten boxes of a funeral home's documents by a road near Puławy; they contained 82 authorisations with personal data of relatives of deceased persons. The boxes had fallen off the open bed of a vehicle during transport and had previously been kept in an unlocked room. The President of UODO found that the controller did not carry out a proper risk analysis, could not show accountability, and did not report the breach to the authority. He imposed a fine of PLN 33,000 and ordered measures to minimise risks within 30 days.
The operator of a mobile application was fined €600 for requiring users to upload a copy of the ID card to attain “verified” status on the platform, in violation of Article 5(1)(c) GDPR.

The AEPD investigated CAMERDATA after an association complained that the data of self-employed people (name, tax ID, address, phone, email) taken from the Chambers of Commerce census was being exposed and sold online. It found that CAMERDATA had no legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR for processing these data. It also found that CAMERDATA did not inform the individuals as Article 14 GDPR requires, and it rejected the 'disproportionate effort' exemption and the general notice on chamber websites. It fined CAMERDATA EUR 200,000 for Article 6(1) and EUR 60,000 for Article 14, and archived the charges about the transfer to KOMPASS and about Article 28. It ordered deletion of the data from the Chamber of Commerce transfer, a halt to processing until a legal basis exists, and individual information to the people concerned.
The DPA fined the Spanish Chamber of Commerce €500,000 for transferring self-employed persons’ tax identity numbers to private companies without a legal basis.

A complaint alleged that data of self-employed persons taken from the AEAT economic activities census were passed to the Chambers of Commerce, CAMERDATA and private companies, and published and used for marketing without proper information. The AEPD found that INFORMA D&B processed the data obtained from CAMERDATA without a valid legal basis (legitimate interest not established) and did not meet the duty to inform data subjects under Article 14. It rejected the company's arguments on nullity, disproportionality and change of criteria, and its claim that one offence was only the means of committing the other. It imposed two fines of EUR 900,000 each (EUR 1.8 million in total) and ordered the company to stop processing the data obtained under the CAMERDATA contract until it has a legal basis, and to delete the data.
The DPA fined a marketing company €42,000 for processing personal data of self-employed persons originating from the Spanish Chamber of Commerce without a legal basis.

A law firm was fined £60,000 (€69,781) for failing to implement appropriate technical and organisational security measures and to notify the DPA within 72 hours after suffering a data breach, in violation of Articles 5(1)(f), 32(1) & 33(1) UK GDPR.
An online store operator was fined €3000 after two customer email complaints were merged, revealing their personal data to each other respectively, in violation of Article 5(1)(f) GDPR.

The DPA fined a company that buys outstanding loans from banks €200,000 for unlawfully including a data subject’s debt in a public credit registry, with the knowledge that said debt had been exonerated two years before in the course of insolvency procedures.

The DPA fined the provider of the “virtual companion” Replika AI €5,000,000 for unlawfully processing personal data, for transparency violations, and for failing to implement effective age verification mechanisms.

Following a report by a TV journalist, the Garante and the Guardia di finanza inspected a network of unauthorised call centres that sold Acea Energia energy contracts using illicitly obtained 'switch-out' contact lists and misleading calls, channelling contracts through an Acea-contracted agency. The Garante found that Acea had allowed promotional calls without consent or information, had de facto entrusted data to a company without a processor appointment, let its staff access Acea systems without designation, and failed to supervise its sales chain. It fined Acea EUR 3,000,000, ordered it to inform all affected data subjects and to check that agencies' sub-agent contracts comply with Article 28, and ordered publication of the decision.

Following a report by a TV journalist, the Garante and the Guardia di Finanza inspected several call centres and agencies selling Acea Energia energy contracts. They found huge purchased contact lists used for promotional calls without valid consent or information notices, missing processor designations under Article 28, unauthorised access to Acea's systems, and in one case incomplete cooperation with the Authority. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, banned the use of the lists found and of any contact lists whose lawfulness cannot be proven, and ordered the five entities to report back within 30 days. It fined them EUR 45,000, 200,000, 500,000, 75,000 and 30,000 (EUR 850,000 in total) and ordered publication of the decision.

A man complained about an unwanted promotional phone call from a real estate agency, which had obtained his contact data from a list broker (Realmaps). The Garante found that the agency, as controller, had not verified or documented consent or information given to the data subjects, had not checked the Public Opposition Register, used a call script lacking Article 13 information, and redirected rights requests to the supplier. It banned further marketing use of the lists, ordered deletion and compliance measures, and fined the agency EUR 15,000.

An employee of the Unione Montana Appennino Parma Est complained about a video surveillance camera at the entrance of the local police command, filmed 24/7 and recorded. The Garante found that the camera, which also films workers, was installed without a union agreement or labour inspectorate authorisation, and that its 'integrated urban security' justification was irrelevant. It also found transparency failings (information notices) and no data protection impact assessment for workers' data. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, fined the Unione EUR 8,000 and ordered it to correct the first-level information sign. The decision is to be published.

Employees of a small municipality complained that individual performance evaluations, with names and scores, were published on the municipality's online notice board and website. The Garante found that about 40 employees' names and scores were disseminated online for 15 days without a suitable legal basis. Neither the municipal regulation, Art. 124 of the local government code nor the transparency decree required named publication; the transparency decree requires only aggregated data. The Garante found a breach of Articles 5 and 6 GDPR and Art. 2-ter of the Code and fined the municipality EUR 4,000, ordering publication of the order on its website. No further corrective measures were needed as the content had been removed.

An estate agency, Undici S.r.l.s., made promotional telephone calls using about 20,881 phone numbers bought from a data supplier (Realmaps), without verifying or documenting consent or the information given to the data subjects, and without checking the Public Opposition Register. It also handled data subjects' requests poorly, depending on the supplier to answer them, and could not show accountability. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, ordered corrective measures and imposed a fine of EUR 8,000, and ordered publication of the decision.

Following a complaint, the Romanian authority investigated Tensa Art Design S.A., owner of the lensa.ro website, which sent marketing SMS messages to the complainant's phone number without proof of consent. The company also failed to handle the complainant's access and erasure requests properly. It was fined RON 49,774 (EUR 10,000) for the lack of a legal basis and RON 24,887 (EUR 5,000) for breaching the data subject rights provisions. Corrective measures were also ordered.

A patient complained against her former private gynaecologist, alleging incomplete access to her medical file, repeated unauthorised access to her electronic health record on the national eHealth platform after the doctor-patient relationship ended, and disclosure of her health data to third parties. The Authority found that the doctor deliberately and repeatedly processed the complainant's health data unlawfully between October 2021 and May 2022, in breach of the lawfulness principle of Article 5(1)(a) GDPR. It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 5,000 under Articles 58(2)(i) and 83(5)(a) GDPR.
The DPA fined a telecommunications company €70,000 for providing inaccurate data in the course of an investigation related to unwanted advertising calls to a data subject.

A complainant said a bank branch employee had signed a data protection and economic activity form in his name, and in his wife's name, for a mortgage enquiry without their consent, and that the marketing and profiling consent boxes were ticked. The AEPD opened a sanctioning procedure against BBVA for breach of the lawfulness principle in Article 6(1) GDPR, with a proposed fine of 200,000 euros. BBVA acknowledged responsibility and paid voluntarily, qualifying for two cumulative 20% reductions. The AEPD terminated the procedure with a reduced fine of 120,000 euros.

The DPA held that the Employment Service rightfully withheld information about the identity of the unintended recipients of a data subject’s personal data in its reply to an access request. The information was unintentionally disclosed to the recipients in course of a data breach.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation of Banca Transilvania in March 2025 after a complaint from an individual. The complainant's mortgage had been paid off, yet a new natural-disaster insurance policy was wrongly issued with an insurer acting for the bank, without consent. The bank had also wrongly requested a significant number of policies, using customers' personal data. The authority found a breach of the lawfulness and fairness principle and the lack of a legal basis, fined the bank 24,883 lei (about EUR 5,000) and ordered it to bring its data collection and further processing into compliance.
A restaurant was fined €500 after unlawfully adding over 200 people to a WhatsApp group to advertise their New Years Eve party without their consent.
The DPA issued a warning to the administrator of a website for refusing to provide the DPA with a list of the persons who followed a user’s profile on the website.

The DPA held that a hospital manager who consults their subordinate's medical file in excess of its internal competences acts as controller for this processing and not the hospital. However, the hospital failed to notify the data breach to the DPA.
The DPA fined a telecommunications company €20,000 for sending a data subject direct marketing without their consent.

On 11 April 2023 Mad Cool launched a web form for ticket holders to confirm their postal details for festival wristbands. The same morning the platform had been moved to a new server with a 2-second micro-cache left active, so for a short time some users saw other users' personal data. The AEPD received six complaints and opened sanction proceedings. It found a breach of the confidentiality principle (Art. 5(1)(f)) and of the security obligation (Art. 32, including the absence of a VPN). It set fines of EUR 2,000 and EUR 1,500, totalling EUR 3,500. The company paid early and waived any administrative appeal (a court challenge remained open), so a 20% reduction applied and the amount paid was EUR 2,800.

Two people complained, one of them a complainant in a workplace harassment investigation, that the company had disclosed the identities of complainants and accused. The company sent the investigation resolutions, naming complainants and accused, to 15 people. The AEPD found a breach of the confidentiality principle in Article 5(1)(f) GDPR. The company admitted responsibility and paid early, so the proposed 200,000 euro fine was reduced by two 20% reductions to 120,000 euros. The AEPD also ordered the company to tell it, within 3 months of the decision becoming final and enforceable, which confidentiality measures it had adopted.

A real estate agency was fined €12,000 after requiring their employees to take photos of mailboxes so that details of the property owners could be included in a database, in violation of Article 6(1) & 14 GDPR.
Following an ex officio investigation, the DPA fined a municipality €3,000 for failing to appoint a data protection officer.

Three employees complained, via their lawyer, about a school's attendance system for administrative staff that used fingerprints combined with a badge. The Garante found that processing biometric data to record attendance had no legal basis, since the 2019 law providing for it had been repealed, and that employee consent cannot cure this given the imbalance in employment. The school had stopped the system and deleted the biometric data, so no further corrective measures were ordered. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and imposed a fine of EUR 4,000, with publication.
A controller was fined £90,000 (€105,412.95) for making over 95,000 unsolicited marketing calls to numbers on a do-not-call list, in violation of national electronic communication legislation.

A ransomware attacker accessed the health and care IT environment of Advanced's AHC division in August 2022 and exfiltrated personal data, including health data, of tens of thousands of people, and healthcare services were disrupted. The ICO found that Advanced, as a processor, failed to implement appropriate security measures under Article 32(1) UK GDPR, with gaps in vulnerability scanning, patch management and multi-factor authentication. It rated the infringement highly serious and negligent, and treated the company's size and responsibility as aggravating, while its incident response and reporting to the NCSC were mitigating. A proposed penalty of £6.09 million was reached, then a settlement gave a 20% reduction and a final penalty of £3,076,320. Advanced agreed not to appeal.

After a cyber attack on NTT DATA Romania's IT infrastructure, personal data of a significant number of people was extracted without authorisation. The authority found the company had not implemented adequate technical and organisational security measures nor regularly tested their effectiveness. It also found the company failed to notify the authority within 72 hours. It fined the company RON 124,432.50 (EUR 25,000) for the security breach and issued a warning for the late notification. The company has paid the fine.
A delivery company was fined €70,000 for delivering a parcel to a third party resulting in the improper disclosure of personal data.

A press release from the Croatian DPA announcing seven fines totalling EUR 169,000. The part relevant to this record concerns a company that used its access to the Ministry of Interior's vehicle registry, granted for another purpose and city, to collect owners' data for parking fee collection for retail chains and a general hospital, without a legal basis. It also had no processor contract with the hospital and failed to take appropriate security measures. The Agency imposed a fine of EUR 80,000 on the company.

This is a press release summarising seven fines totalling EUR 169,000 issued by the Croatian DPA. The part matching this Fino entry concerns a company that publicly published data on craftsmen online, collected from public registers and financial data obtained under a contract. The Agency found no proven legal basis for publishing the data or keeping data of deregistered craftsmen permanently, a lack of transparency, a deficient record of processing activities and a data protection officer with a conflict of interest (also the director). It imposed an administrative fine of EUR 40,000.

The press release summarises seven fines issued by the Croatian DPA totalling EUR 169,000. The part relevant to this entry concerns the Clinical Hospital Centre Zagreb, which suffered a cyber attack after an attacker, probably using social engineering, gained VPN access and used an outdated operating system to obtain domain admin rights, copying at least 3 GB of data over 7 days. The Agency found insufficient technical security measures and multiple failings in system design (access restriction, monitoring, reporting, timely reaction), and imposed a fine of EUR 20,000.

A press release of 24 March 2025 summarising seven administrative fines totalling EUR 169,000 issued by the Croatian DPA. The part relevant to this record concerns General Hospital Zadar, which used a company's application that automatically pulled vehicle owners' data from the Ministry of Interior web service without a legal basis to issue daily parking tickets. The hospital also failed to inform parking users properly, did not take appropriate organisational measures, and had no processing contract with the company as processor. A fine of EUR 4,000 was imposed. The same release covers other fines (parking company, data publisher, KBC Zagreb, Vinkovci hospital, a casino and an oil producer) that are not part of this record.

This is a press release from the Croatian DPA announcing seven new administrative fines totalling EUR 169,000. Only a short passage concerns the casino: it and an oil and fat producer were fined for failing to comply with the GDPR rules on appointing and positioning a data protection officer. The casino received EUR 12,000 and the producer EUR 10,000. The other fines in the release (parking data, public disclosure of data, hospitals) are separate cases.

A press release from the Croatian DPA announces seven new administrative fines totalling EUR 169,000. This record concerns one of them: a fine of EUR 10,000 on an oil and fat manufacturing company for failing to comply with the rules on appointing and positioning a data protection officer. A casino received a EUR 12,000 fine for the same type of issue. The release gives no further detail on the oil and fat company's case.

The DPA fined a real estate investor two fines of RON 4,977 each (EUR 2,000 in all) for failing to prove consent to the use of personal data for telemarketing, and for failing to respond to data access requests.
A DPA held that a controller processed a former employee's personal data unlawfully by redirecting the emails sent to their old work email account to another account.
A football club was fined €600 after disposing of a large number of documents in a bin on a public road. The documents contained the personal data of minors playing for the club.

The UODO President opened proceedings of its own motion over the disclosure of data from the PESEL population register on 22 April 2020 to a state-owned postal company, for the planned postal-vote presidential election. It found that the Minister of Digital Affairs disclosed the data of all adult Polish citizens (PESEL number, names, addresses) without a legal basis, breaching Article 6(1) and the lawfulness principle in Article 5(1)(a). It fined the Minister PLN 100,000, the statutory maximum for public bodies. The same decision found the postal company processed the data unlawfully and fined it PLN 27,124,816. Only the Minister's part is summarised here.
The DPA fined a bank €1,600,000 for attempting to verify the origin of funds to be deposited by a prospective customer without a legal basis under Article 6(1) GDPR.

Carrefour notified the Spanish authority of five personal data breaches in which attackers gained unauthorised access to customer accounts on its website and the MiCarrefour app. The AEPD found that Carrefour breached the integrity and confidentiality principle (Art. 5(1)(f)), failed to apply adequate security measures (Art. 32) and failed to properly notify affected individuals (Art. 34). It imposed fines of EUR 2,000,000, EUR 1,000,000 and EUR 200,000 respectively, a total of EUR 3,200,000. It also ordered Carrefour to communicate the breaches to the affected individuals within one month of the decision becoming final. Carrefour accepted responsibility only for the Art. 34 infringement and asked for reductions, but these were not applied because it neither paid nor waived appeals.

A man started an online Vodafone fixed-line offer and abandoned it. A Vodafone dealer, G@S, phoned him, got him to send his ID document via WhatsApp and used it to register a different activation in Vodafone's systems. The Garante found G@S had exceeded its role as processor and acted as an autonomous controller without a legal basis, consent or privacy notice. It banned further processing of the complainant's data and fined G@S EUR 15,000, with publication of the order.

Three former employees of a bankrupt company complained that Encore Thermoengineering, which bought part of the business together with its email domain and servers, kept their individual mailboxes active, redirected incoming mail to its managing director and refused to delete the data. The Garante found that keeping the server and backup indefinitely, reading the messages and redirecting all mail breached lawfulness, data minimisation and storage limitation, and that the erasure requests were not properly answered. It ordered erasure of the individual mailbox data (save for retention needed for legal claims), ordered the redirection system to be brought into compliance within 60 days, and fined the company EUR 20,000.

A customer complained that Interflora Italia kept sending him promotional SMS messages after guest purchases on its e-commerce site, where giving a mobile number was mandatory and no consent for marketing was requested. His objection and access request to the company's DPO went unanswered, and the company also ignored the Garante's requests for information. The Garante found unlawful processing (no valid consent, breach of fairness, transparency and purpose limitation, failure to answer data subject rights requests). Because the company had remedied everything during the proceedings, it imposed no corrective measures but ordered a fine of EUR 40,000 and publication of the decision.

The DPA rejected a police officer's complaint seeking the de-indexing of news articles concerning their criminal convictions. The DPA held that the articles were accurate, up to date, and of general interest due to the complainant's position as a public officer.

ANSPDCP concluded an investigation in February 2025 at Automobilus International S.R.L., started after the company notified a personal data breach. A third party had illegally accessed the customer database by exploiting a vulnerability on one of the company's servers. The authority found the company had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational security measures and breached Article 32(1) and (2) GDPR. It fined the company 24,885 lei (about EUR 5,000) and ordered it to inform affected individuals about the incident and the remedial measures through a notice on its website's front page.
An accommodation provider was fined €1,200 for infringing Article 5(1)(c) GDPR by requiring guests, including children, to send photos of their IDs via WhatsApp.

The UODO President inspected Polskie Radio Szczecin after a 2022 news item identified a child victim of sexual abuse, who later took their own life. The inspection found no risk analysis for editorial processing, no procedure for checking press material for personal data before publication, no encryption of portable media, and no regular testing of security measures. The President ordered the radio to fix these organisational and technical failings within 60 days and imposed an administrative fine of PLN 56,824. The fine was kept lower because of the weak finances of public regional broadcasters.

The Bulgarian CPDP stated that personal data posted on social media by the organizer constitutes valid consent under GDPR Art. 6(1)(a) for processing by others, as the data subject voluntarily submitted the data to the petitioner.

Datatilsynet inspected Telenor ASA's data protection officer arrangements and internal control. It found that the company had not made the necessary assessments and documentation on the DPO role and had not set up a documented reporting line to top management. It also found that the company lacked suitable organisational measures and policies. The authority fined Telenor ASA NOK 4,000,000 for breaching Article 24(1) and (2) GDPR, and ordered it to assess and document whether it must have a DPO and to correct its records of processing. It also issued a reprimand for the inadequate reporting line. The decision was adopted under the Article 60 cooperation procedure with the Swedish and Danish authorities as concerned authorities.

The DPA fined a bank €10,000 for storing inaccurate data of the data subject beyond the statutory retention period. As well as for failing to implement meaningful and effective measures to ensure compliance with the GDPR.
The DPA fined a news outlet PLN 56,824 (€13,500) for failing to implement appropriate security measures. Amongst others, the DPA found a failure to review and update the risk analysis.

The DPA fined an e-billing website RON 99,518 (€20,000) for failing to conduct regular security assessments in violation of Article 32 GDPR. This failure led to a cyberattack which allowed a third party to access personal data (e.g. bank account numbers).

ANSPDCP finished an investigation in January 2025 into WEBRASOFT SRL, which ran an online invoicing site. An attacker illegally accessed the server holding the customer database, exposing personal data of a large number of customers. The company had not regularly tested and evaluated the effectiveness of its security measures. It was fined 99,518 lei (about EUR 20,000) for breaching Article 32 GDPR and ordered to set up access logging on its servers. The company has paid the fine.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation into BEKO România SA, started after a personal data breach notification. An unauthorised person exploited a programming vulnerability to access the website holding the customer database. The authority found the company had not applied appropriate technical and organisational measures nor regularly tested their effectiveness. It fined the company 49,766 lei (about EUR 10,000) and ordered it to implement a data volume analysis system with back-ups. The company has paid the fine.

A gym customer complained that instructors at a gym of the SCHOOL FITNESS group filmed classes without informing participants or obtaining valid consent. The company said members expressly consent in their sign-up contract. In its opening decision, which the resolution confirms, the AEPD found that the sign-up contracts, at least as of 13 April 2022, mention no clause on the general use of clients' images, and that the later terms and the online sign-up it checked in January 2025 made signing up conditional on accepting the section on images, so the clients' consent was flawed. The AEPD opened sanction proceedings against the parent company for infringing Articles 7, 5(1)(e) and 28 GDPR, proposing fines of EUR 15,000, 15,000 and 6,000 (EUR 36,000 in total). The company acknowledged responsibility and paid voluntarily on 11 March 2025, receiving two 20% reductions, so the reduced fine is EUR 21,600. The AEPD declared the infringements, confirmed the sanctions, closed the procedure and ordered the company to adopt corrective measures within 6 months.
The DPA fined a junior football club €600 as the consent collected from parents for the taking of photographs of their child was not freely given, thus violating Article 7 GDPR.

The DPA held that a real estate agency infringed a data subject’s right to privacy by publishing unpixelated drone images of her home. The images were considered personal data under the GDPR and their publication was unnecessary for marketing purposes.

The Italian DPA investigated the energy supplier Energia Pulita S.r.l. after receiving 82 reports of unsolicited telemarketing calls made without a valid legal basis. It found unlawful processing without proper legal basis or consent, inadequate technical and organisational measures, failures in choosing, instructing and monitoring the sales agencies and sub-agencies it used, and defective information notices. The Garante banned further processing of the reporting persons' data and ordered the company to inform 68 affected people, to put in place controls on its sales network, and to report back within thirty days. It imposed a fine of EUR 300,000 and published the decision as an ancillary sanction.

The DPA issued a warning against a company for failing to respond timely to a former employee's access request. The DPA clarified that the right of access applies to all personal data, including information already known to the data subject.

A customer complained that on 25 January 2023 a fraudulent SIM duplicate was issued on his line by Vodafone, after which two fraudulent bank transfers were made from his account. Vodafone said it cancelled the duplicate the same day and argued it was not at fault. The AEPD found that Vodafone processed the complainant's data without a legal basis, in breach of Article 6(1) GDPR, because its agent did not carry out the required verification. It imposed a fine of EUR 200,000, treating Vodafone's earlier fines under Article 6(1) as aggravating.

Ibermutua's online platform for employer clients sent weekly sick-leave emails that, due to a programming error, attached Excel files containing health-related data of employees of other companies. Several complaints were lodged with the AEPD in August and September 2024. The AEPD opened a sanctions procedure for breach of the integrity and confidentiality principle, with a proposed fine of EUR 1,000,000. Ibermutua admitted responsibility and paid voluntarily, obtaining two cumulative 20% reductions, so the final fine is EUR 600,000, and it must report on security measures within 3 months.

The Icelandic DPA opened an own-initiative investigation into the shared electronic health record system of the Primary Health Care in the Capital Area. The organisation had given eleven other bodies (other clinics, a football association, an aviation medical centre, the transport authority, the labour directorate, municipal services) access to patient records without the minister's licence and the DPA's security confirmation required by Article 20 of the Patient Records Act. The DPA found it had not shown the processing was lawful under the GDPR (Arts 5, 6, 9) and fined it ISK 5,000,000. No corrective orders were issued because it had applied for the licences and closed the unauthorised accesses.

The DPA found that a controller violated Article 17(1)(c) GDPR by failing to timely comply with an erasure request by a previous subscriber to its newsletter. Although the data were eventually deleted, the delay constituted an infringement.

The Italian DPA investigated a company that offers out-of-court assistance to investors. It had obtained a list of a bank's shareholders from another shareholder and sent about 15,000 paper letters promoting its meetings and collective action. The Garante found no valid legal basis (legitimate interest was not enough, consent was needed for promotional contact), no proper Article 14 information, and no replies to data subject requests. Because the company cooperated, changed its practices and stopped the mailings, the Garante ordered only a ban on further use of the shareholder list. It also imposed a fine of EUR 15,000 and ordered publication of the decision.

An individual (controller) was ordered to delete photos of individuals that they had taken and published online. The photos included those of children, one taken from an angle revealing a woman’s cleavage, one revealing the subjects’ religious beliefs, and one of people dining in a restaurant.

The DPA found that a website, controlled by the State Education Development Agency, placed marketing and analytics cookies without visitors' consent and without providing information about the processing of personal data. The DPA ordered the Agency to bring the use of cookies into compliance.

In the context of a dismissed complaint about satisfaction surveys, the DPA referred to the recent CJEU case C-394/23 Mousse to confirm that unnecessary processing of the gender of the data subject threatens compliance with the principle of data minimisation.

ANSPDCP concluded an investigation into Omniasig Vienna Insurance Group S.A. after receiving a personal data breach notification under Article 33 GDPR. The investigation revealed that an employee of a data processor improperly accessed claim files and used the personal and health data of insured clients to file fraudulent compensation claims. The authority determined that the controller failed to implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure data security and integrity under Article 32(1), (2), and (4) GDPR. Consequently, ANSPDCP imposed a fine of RON 14,931 (EUR 3,000) and ordered the controller to establish an inspection and audit plan for the processor to avoid similar incidents.

The DPA fined a Bank €3,000 for a failure to implement appropriate security measures following an internal data breach. An employee had wrongfully retained administrator rights and accessed the data of over 6,000 other employees without authorization.
The DPA imposed a fine of €1,000 on an individual for unlawfully transmitting personal data to ecclesiastical authorities regarding data subjects not subject to the competency of those authorities.
A processor was fined €500,000 after appointing sub-processors without authorisation from the controller in violation of Article 28(2) GDPR.

ANSPDCP completed an investigation in December 2024 into FARMEC SA after the company notified a personal data breach. A cyber attack accessed a database of users and administrators of its website and data was extracted. The company had not implemented the necessary security measures or updated its systems to the latest licensed version. The authority found breaches of Articles 25(1) and 32(1)(b), (d) and (2) GDPR and fined the company 24,854.50 lei (about EUR 5,000), which it has paid.

The DPA held that a person receiving care in their home could not base the recording of care workers via CCTV on their legitimate interest. The DPA ordered the shutoff of the cameras during the care workers' visits.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in December 2024 into an accounting and management company after a complaint. The company did not answer the authority's requests for information. It also sent a table of access passwords to the Revisal platform for several legal entities to a third party over WhatsApp, giving unauthorised access to employees' personal data. The company received two fines, 2,000 EUR and 8,000 EUR (10,000 EUR in total), and was ordered to change all Revisal access credentials for the affected entities.

The Romanian DPA closed an investigation into Unicredit Bank SA in December 2024, started after the bank sent two personal data breach notifications. Two breaches resulted from applications or communication solutions that were put into use without adequate prior testing in a test environment, exposing customers' personal and financial data without authorisation. The authority found a breach of Article 25(1) GDPR and fined the bank RON 74,652 (EUR 15,000). It also ordered the bank to put in place a testing plan for all components handling personal data. The bank has already paid the fine.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation in December 2024 into Hidroelectrica, started after the company notified a personal data breach. The breach occurred when the company's application was launched, because of a technical error and insufficient testing in an environment simulating real use. This caused loss of integrity and availability and unauthorised disclosure or access affecting a significant number of data subjects. The authority found a breach of Article 25(1) and (2) GDPR and fined the company 74,562 lei (about EUR 15,000). It also ordered a technical and procedural test plan simulating real production scenarios before launching new components. The fine has been paid.
The DPA issued a warning against a bank for providing belated and incomplete responses to data subjects' access requests.

The DPA issued a reprimand to a controller for failing to identify a legal basis prior to processing. Furthermore, it held that personal data could be necessary for the performance of a television service contract.

The Romanian DPA finished an investigation into Orange România in December 2024. After a failed attempt to subscribe to mobile services, a person asked for all their data to be erased, but the operator asked for more personal data and gave incomplete answers. The operator also excessively collected and stored scanned identity documents no longer needed for identification. It received two fines of RON 99,510 (EUR 20,000) each, totalling RON 199,020 (EUR 40,000), plus corrective measures.

The DPA dismissed numerous challenges to the admissibility of complaints facilitated by noyb. The DPA found that the mere fact that data subjects were noyb volunteers couldn't in and of itself show that there was no legitimate, direct and personal interest at hand.
The DPA held that offering to show the data subject their personal data at a meeting was not an adequate response to an access request.
The DPA reprimanded an online broker for failing to adequately explain to a data subject the reasons for not complying with their erasure request, in violation of Article 12(4) GDPR.

Following several investigations completed in December 2024, the Romanian authority found that Vodafone Romania repeatedly failed to keep customer data confidential because staff or processors did not follow internal data-handling policies. Incidents included sending an invoice photo to a third party, not using BCC in group emails, sharing a screenshot via WhatsApp, and sending an invoice to the wrong person. The controller was fined RON 74,526 (about EUR 15,000) for breaching Article 32(4) with Article 32(1)(b) GDPR. The operator has paid the fine.

The DPA held that the implementation of an optional facial-recognition system, used to efficiently manage access to a football stadium, violated the principle of data minimisation as there were less invasive alternatives and therefore issued a €200,000 fine.

The DPA fined an adult entertainment provider €10,000 for processing a pornographic video because it based the processing on the performance of a contract which the data subject had not been a party to.

The Italian DPA received many complaints from people who got marketing calls from real estate agencies that said they got their data from Realmaps. An inspection in April 2024 showed Realmaps sold lists of property owners with phone numbers, built from list providers' data and land registry data, without checking consent or giving information notices. The DPA held Realmaps was an independent controller, not a mere intermediary, and found violations on legal basis, transparency, accountability, processor and authorised-person designation, security, records, DPIA and DPO. It banned processing on lists lacking valid consent, imposed corrective orders and a fine of EUR 100,000, and ordered publication.
The DPA fined a hospital €6,000 for unlawfully disclosing employees' health data by sending it to a shared email account.

The DPA found a local business in breach of GDPR for the non-compliant installation of security cameras. The DPA fined data controller for €1,500, and ordered to provide information on processing and to stop the filming of public spaces

The DPA imposed a €5,000 fine on a Municipality for violating the data minimisation principle by publishing a school committee’s decision containing personal data on its website that exceeded what was necessary for journalistic purposes.

The DPA fined a solar panel provider €42,000 for sending contractual documents to all participants of a solar neighbourhood project. In violation of the principle of data minimisation, these documents unnecessarily contained personal information of all participants.

The DPA reprimanded a bank for failing to explain why it didn’t provide a complete copy of personal data after a data subject’s access request. Further, the DPA ordered the bank to provide additional documents in a redacted format.

Two customers complained that a payment sent to one of them through the bank's i-bank Pay app was credited to the other, unrelated customer, and that the bank did not answer their access requests. An on-site audit by the Authority showed a software error during the June 2020 integration of IRIS pay into Mobile Banking, which activated phone numbers that had never been verified by OTP. The bank then notified a personal data breach. It found 24 further affected customers and 38 erroneous transfers totalling EUR 2,149.66. The Authority fined the bank EUR 100,000 for the breaches of Articles 5(1)(d) and (f) with 32, and of Articles 25, 33 and 34, and EUR 20,000 for the breach of the Article 15 access right.

The Authority examined seven complaints against the National Bank of Greece about late or missing responses to data subjects' access requests, mostly for recordings of phone calls after fraud incidents. Replies came months late, and the bank blamed remote-working arrangements and request volumes. For the first complainant, whose recordings were withheld while the bank used them in a court dispute, it fined the bank EUR 20,000 under Article 15. For the other six complaints it issued a reprimand under Articles 12(3)-(4) and 15. In its own-initiative audit it found that the bank had no adequate procedures for handling access requests (Articles 12(2) and 25(1)) and fined it EUR 200,000.

The DPA reprimanded an employer for unlawfully processing allegations regarding the assault of a minor by an employee in the context of a disciplinary action. The controller was ordered to implement appropriate measures to ensure future GDPR compliance.

The DPA investigated a complaint concerning a breach of the right of access to personal data including recorded conversations concerning the complaint against a loan and credit management company. Subsequently, it issued a fine.

The CNPD's restricted formation concluded an investigation into an anonymised controller (Société A) over how it handled data subject requests. It found that the controller failed to answer 47 requests within the deadlines in Article 12(3) and (4) GDPR, and counted this as 46 breaches. It issued a reprimand and an administrative fine of EUR 175,000. The fine was calculated using the EDPB's 2023 fine calculation guidelines. The authority treated the breach as being of low gravity, but still considered a fine necessary to deter other controllers and to keep sanctioning consistent. The investigation head had proposed a fine of EUR 493,560.

The DPA fined a bank €50,000 after its processor unlawfully disclosed personal data of its customer to an impersonator even though the impersonator could not correctly answer identity verification questions.

The DPA fined the telecom company Wind Tre €347,520 for its aggressive marketing practices, i.e. using contact data from consumers who had no previous interaction with the company without their consent.

The DPA held that appointing a procurator of a company as a DPO constitutes a conflict of interest and thus a violation of Article 38(6) GDPR. For this and the failure to name the DPO in accordance with Article 37(6) GDPR on the company's website, the DPA fined the company €12,000.

The Dutch DPA had fined Coolblue in a primary decision of 11 January 2024 for processing personal data through tracking cookies without valid consent, because its cookie banner assumed tacit consent and used pre-ticked boxes. In this decision on objection, the AP declared the objection well-founded and revoked the primary decision. It still found the infringement of Articles 5(1)(a) and 6(1) GDPR, covering 28 April to 17 June 2020, and imposed a new fine of EUR 40,000. The fine was set far below the category II starting point of EUR 310,000 because of the low seriousness of the infringement, the way the infringement was ended, unclear remedy period and the long time between the start of the procedure and the primary decision.

A man asked Línea Directa for a car insurance quote and was phoned by an agent of its processor, Majorel. Without his consent, the agent checked his driving licence points balance on the traffic authority (DGT) website, using an email address that was not his to obtain the access key. The AEPD found that Línea Directa had no legal basis for the points check, which was not necessary for the contract, and that its contractual arrangements with Majorel did not meet Article 28 GDPR. It fined the insurer EUR 100,000 for Article 6(1) and EUR 200,000 for Article 28, and ordered it to bring its processing and its processor contracts into line within three months.

During a rebuild of Panek SA's website, a subcontractor's employee mistakenly placed files with customer data from the old site on the new one, and Google indexed them, making them publicly accessible. About 21,453 customers and employees were affected. The Polish DPA found that Panek had not implemented appropriate technical and organisational measures based on a risk analysis, had not tested their effectiveness, and had not supervised the processor. It fined Panek PLN 1,527,855 and its processor ITCenter PLN 20,037.

The Spanish DPA investigated the professional football league LNFP (LaLiga) over a biometric (fingerprint) recognition system used to give season-ticket holders access to the 'animation stands' of first- and second-division stadiums. It found that the league, as controller, had not carried out a data protection impact assessment (DPIA) as required by Article 35 GDPR. It fined the league EUR 1,000,000, taking into account the league's arguments about audiovisual rights management and its turnover. It also ordered the league to suspend the biometric access system until a valid DPIA is carried out and passed, and to pass this suspension on to the affiliated clubs.
The DPA fined a business information publisher €40,000 and held that they erred in failing to regard information about sole proprietors as personal data and found numerous GDPR violations.

The French data protection authority (CNIL) sanctioned a real estate company for implementing unlawful employee monitoring tools, including the Time Doctor activity-monitoring software for teleworking staff and an in-office video surveillance system. The CNIL found breaches of Articles 5(1)(c), 6, 12, 13, 32, and 35 of the GDPR resulting from disproportionate worker surveillance, lack of legal basis and information, security deficiencies, and failure to conduct a Data Protection Impact Assessment (DPIA). Taking into account the gravity and intentional or negligent character of the violations alongside mitigating factors such as the company's cooperation and prompt deactivation of the software, the CNIL imposed a €40,000 fine. The decision was also ordered to be published on the CNIL and Légifrance websites without identifying the company by name.

After press reports, the Italian DPA opened an ex officio investigation into the municipality of Brescia. Fetuses and aborted products were buried at the Vantiniano cemetery with grave markers showing a first name 'XX' and a surname that often matched the woman's, and the same data could be searched on the municipal cemetery web portal labelled 'fetuses and stillborn'. This amounted to disclosure of health data without a valid legal basis and breached the principles of lawfulness, purpose limitation, minimisation and accuracy. The Garante declared the processing unlawful and fined the municipality EUR 10,000, taking account of the corrective measures already taken, and ordered it to confirm within 30 days that the portal shows only permitted data. The decision is to be published.

The Italian DPA inspected a credit-rehabilitation company after the Bank of Italy reported that its legal representative had made many credit-register access requests without proper authority. The inspection found no retention rules (data of tens of thousands of clients kept indefinitely in a single CRM), missing Article 28 contracts with processors, a DPO designated but not notified to the authority, and transparency and accountability failures. The company also ignored the authority's request for information and filed no defence. The Garante declared the processing unlawful, ordered corrective measures within 90 days and imposed a fine of EUR 70,000, with publication of the decision.

The DPA reprimanded a gambling company for the improper design of their cookie banner. The graphical emphasis of the accept option and the additional steps required to refuse cookies made the consent under Article 6 GDPR invalid.

The DPA has granted F.C. Copenhagen’s application to use facial recognition technology at football matches under national law since the intended enforcement of suspensions is a substantial public interest. No permission was given for non-football events.

An investor in real estate projects managed by the company complained that, when he asked for information about the projects, the company asked for a copy of his national ID without telling him how his data would be processed. After a sanction procedure, the AEPD found that the company breached Article 13 GDPR (failure to inform) and Article 32.1 GDPR (no appropriate security measures, since it asked for scanned ID by email). It imposed two fines of EUR 50,000 each and ordered the company to bring its processing into line within six months of the decision becoming final. The company did not answer the authority's information requests, and the AEPD rejected its proportionality and 'acting on behalf of a third party' arguments.

The DPA found, that a financial institution did not guarantee its DPO's independence. In addition, the institution failed to properly document its credit scoring activities. Thus the DPA imposed a total fine of ca. €132,000 (PLN 576,220).
The DPA found that Google LLC and Google Ireland Ltd. are joint controllers for the processing of personal data in connection with Google services in the EEA.

The Irish DPC announced two final decisions against Meta Platforms Ireland following own-volition inquiries into a 2018 breach in which attackers exploited Facebook user tokens, affecting about 29 million accounts globally (about 3 million in the EU/EEA). The DPC found infringements of Articles 33(3), 33(5), 25(1) and 25(2) GDPR, issued reprimands and ordered administrative fines totalling €251 million. The individual fines were €8 million, €3 million, €130 million and €110 million. No objections were raised to the draft decision under the Article 60 cooperation procedure.

The DPA fined a loan comparison service provider €950,000 for making loan applications available to the public without implementing appropriate safeguards, thus violating the principle of integrity and confidentiality.

A Belgian hospital notified the DPA of a ransomware attack in 2021 that made systems, medical records and emergency care unavailable for days. After an inspection, the Litigation Chamber found failures in security measures, no data protection impact assessment, and breaches of integrity and confidentiality and accountability. It fined the hospital EUR 200,000 after reducing a starting amount for the hospital's financial difficulties, the COVID context and the energy crisis, and ordered compliance measures within 90 days. The Market Court on 3 September 2025 partly annulled the decision and cut the fine to EUR 50,000; the DPA has appealed in cassation.
The DPA fined a newspaper €10,000 for failing to make use of anonymization techniques in order to minimise the personal data shown in a video that was part of an online article.
The EDPS issued a reprimand to the European Commission for unlawfully targeting X users based on their political views in order to promote a legislative proposal.
